claim: The theta rhythm is a quasi-periodic 4–10 Hz oscillation observed during memory processing in the hippocampus.
source: The theta rhythm, a quasi-periodic 4–10 Hz oscillation, is observed during memory processing in the hippocampus, with different phases of theta hypothesized to separate independent streams of information related to the encoding and recall of memories.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about theta oscillations in the hippocampus, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Different phases of theta are hypothesized to separate independent streams of information related to the encoding and recall of memories.
source: The theta rhythm, a quasi-periodic 4–10 Hz oscillation, is observed during memory processing in the hippocampus, with different phases of theta hypothesized to separate independent streams of information related to the encoding and recall of memories.
evidence: This is a hypothesis referenced from the literature, particularly the SPEAR model.

claim: Certain memories are stored, in part, in a sparse ensemble of neurons in the hippocampus.
source: At the cellular level, the discovery of hippocampal memory cells (engram neurons), as well as the modulation of memory recall through optogenetic activation of these cells, has provided evidence that certain memories are stored, in part, in a sparse ensemble of neurons in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on engram neurons.

claim: Engram reactivation has been carried out using open-loop stimulation at fixed frequencies without considering ongoing network oscillations.
source: In previous research, however, engram reactivation has been carried out using open-loop stimulation at fixed frequencies; the relationship between engram neuron reactivation and ongoing network oscillations has not been taken into consideration.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research methods.

claim: Stimulating dentate gyrus engram neurons at the trough of theta is more effective in eliciting behavioral recall than fixed-frequency stimulation or stimulation at the peak of theta.
source: Consistent with previously hypothesized functions of theta oscillations in memory function, we show that stimulating dentate gyrus engram neurons at the trough of theta is more effective in eliciting behavioral recall than either fixed-frequency stimulation or stimulation at the peak of theta.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phase-specific trough stimulation is accompanied by an increase in the coupling between gamma and theta oscillations in CA1 hippocampus.
source: Moreover, phase-specific trough stimulation is accompanied by an increase in the coupling between gamma and theta oscillations in CA1 hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the modulation index analysis presented in the results.

claim: The results provide a causal link between phase-specific activation of engram cells and the behavioral expression of memory.
source: Our results provide a causal link between phase-specific activation of engram cells and the behavioral expression of memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing that trough stimulation causes increased freezing behavior.

claim: Engram cells are neurons whose activity correlates with memory activity.
source: The discovery of neurons whose activity correlates with memory activity, often referred to as engram cells, has offered evidence that certain memories are stored in a sparse set of neuronal ensembles across the hippocampus (Reijmers et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Engram cells are active during the encoding of a memory and reactivate upon recall of that specific event.
source: These cells are active during the encoding of a memory and reactivate upon recall of that specific event (Denny et al., 2014; Tayler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a characteristic of engram cells supported by citations.

claim: Artificial reactivation of engram neurons induces recall-like behavior, establishing a causal role for these neurons in memory processing.
source: Further, artificial reactivation of engram neurons induces recall-like behavior, thus establishing a causal role for these neurons in memory processing (Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Activity-based neural tagging strategies link expression of a protein of interest to the expression of immediate early genes.
source: Previous studies have utilized activity-based neural tagging strategies, which link expression of a protein of interest (e.g. Channelrhodopsin) to the expression of immediate early genes (IEG) (most commonly Arc [Denny et al., 2014] and cFos [Liu et al., 2012]) to tag and modulate active populations during a specific event.
evidence: This describes a methodology supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hippocampus is a brain structure in the temporal lobe with a modular design consisting of three major sub-regions: the dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, and CA1.
source: The modulation of memories through activity-based tagging of engram neurons has often targeted cells in the hippocampus (Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020; Tonegawa et al., 2015); a brain structure in the temporal lobe with a modular design that consists of three major sub-regions: the dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, and CA1, all with extensive interconnectivity (Andersen et al., 2009; Squire et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There have been discrepancies in the most effective stimulation frequency for driving engram neurons in different regions of the hippocampus.
source: In these studies, however, there have been discrepancies in the most effective stimulation frequency, both between regions and within regions (cCompare Ohkawa et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation about the literature supported by citations.

claim: Studies have been limited to activating engram neurons using fixed-frequency stimulation, without taking into consideration the ongoing spontaneous network activity.
source: Further, studies have been limited to activating engram neurons using fixed-frequency stimulation, without taking into consideration the ongoing spontaneous network activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: Hippocampal regions are dominated by a quasi-periodic 4–10 Hz network-wide theta oscillation in the field potential generated by temporally organized firing during memory processing.
source: In particular, hippocampal regions are dominated by a quasi-periodic 4–10 Hz network-wide theta oscillation in the field potential generated by temporally organized firing during memory processing (Buzsáki, 2002; Colgin, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hippocampal oscillations supported by citations.

claim: The SPEAR model posits that encoding and retrieval are temporally interleaved at different phases of hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: A prominent model, termed the Separate Phase of Encoding and Recall (SPEAR) model (Hasselmo et al., 2002), posits that encoding and retrieval are temporally interleaved at different phases of hippocampal theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model supported by citation.

claim: In the SPEAR model, the peak of the hippocampal theta oscillation is dominated by inputs from the entorhinal cortex, which carry sensory information potentially required for the encoding process.
source: In the SPEAR model (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Hasselmo and Stern, 2014), the peak of the hippocampal theta oscillation (as measured in striatum pyramidale) is dominated by inputs from the entorhinal cortex, which carry sensory information that is potentially required for the encoding process.
evidence: This is a description of the SPEAR model supported by citations.

claim: In the SPEAR model, the trough of theta oscillations occurs during strong CA3 activity, a region known for pattern completion supported through strong recurrent connections.
source: In contrast, the trough (negative peak) of theta oscillations occurs during strong CA3 activity, a region of the hippocampus known for pattern completion that is supported through strong recurrent connections (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Rolls, 2016; Senzai, 2019), and thus ideally suited for the retrieval of previously stored memories.
evidence: This is a description of the SPEAR model supported by citations.

claim: The SPEAR model has been supported by electrophysiological data in vivo and in vitro.
source: The SPEAR model has been supported by electrophysiological data in vivo (Hyman et al., 2003; Kerrén et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020) and in vitro (Kwag and Paulsen, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about empirical support for the SPEAR model, supported by citations.

claim: The peak of theta oscillations is associated with strong long-term potentiation, which can support the encoding process.
source: These studies have indicated that the peak of theta oscillations is associated with strong long-term potentiation, which can support the encoding process, while the trough of theta has strong long-term depression that supports the recall of previously stored memories (Douchamps et al., 2013; Manns et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: The trough of theta has strong long-term depression that supports the recall of previously stored memories.
source: These studies have indicated that the peak of theta oscillations is associated with strong long-term potentiation, which can support the encoding process, while the trough of theta has strong long-term depression that supports the recall of previously stored memories (Douchamps et al., 2013; Manns et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: In behaving mice, memory performance can be altered through phase-specific inhibition of neurons in CA1.
source: In behaving mice, memory performance can be altered through phase-specific inhibition of neurons in CA1, the output region of the hippocampus (Siegle and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: A recent study in human subjects has shown a strong correlation between memory tasks and the phase of theta.
source: Finally, a recent study in human subjects has shown a strong correlation between memory tasks and the phase of theta (Kragel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: The activation of engram neurons has been carried out at fixed frequencies, without taking into account the phase of theta oscillations.
source: Despite these results, as well as the prior development of closed-loop optogenetics stimulation (Grosenick et al., 2015), the activation of engram neurons has been carried out at fixed frequencies, without taking into account the phase of theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: The study implemented a real-time phase prediction algorithm to test the behavioral and electrophysiological effects of theta-phase-specific stimulation of DG memory neurons.
source: To test this hypothesis, we implemented a real-time phase prediction algorithm and tested the behavioral and electrophysiological effects of theta-phase-specific stimulation of DG memory neurons in gating memory recall.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the current study.

claim: Theta was measured in CA1 to be consistent with past literature and the SPEAR model.
source: We measured theta in CA1 to be consistent with past literature and the SPEAR model.
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained by the authors.

claim: Memory neurons were tagged and reactivated in DG rather than CA3 because reactivation of tagged CA3 neurons is not well studied and tends to generate seizure-like activity.
source: We tagged and reactivated memory neurons in DG rather than CA3, as would be ideal in a test of the SPEAR model. We did this because reactivation of tagged CA3 neurons is not well studied and tends to generate seizure-like activity (unpublished data), presumably because of the higher probability of connection among CA3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained by the authors, with reference to unpublished observations.

claim: DG stimulation causes robust behavior without generating seizure-like activity.
source: In contrast, DG stimulation causes robust behavior without generating seizure-like activity.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: The results of phase-specific stimulation were compared with fixed-frequency stimulation at 20 Hz and 6 Hz.
source: We compared the results of phase-specific stimulation with those using fixed-frequency stimulation at the previously established value of 20 Hz, as well as stimulation at 6 Hz, which provided a control representing the average stimulation frequency during phase-specific activation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The results support the SPEAR model.
source: Our results support the SPEAR model, with optogenetic stimulation of engram neurons in DG at the trough (recall) phase driving the most robust behavioral recall and the largest amount of coupling between the theta and gamma rhythms in CA1 region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Most studies have used 20 Hz stimulation for engram reactivation, which is well above the natural firing rates measured in the DG.
source: To date, engram work has used fixed-frequency optogenetic stimulation to reactivate tagged cells and drive behavior linked to memory recall. For example, most studies have used 20 Hz stimulation, which is well above the natural firing rates measured in the DG (1 Hz on average, with peak rates of 8 Hz) (GoodSmith et al., 2017; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research methods supported by citations.

claim: The average firing rate in DG is 1 Hz, with peak rates of 8 Hz.
source: For example, most studies have used 20 Hz stimulation, which is well above the natural firing rates measured in the DG (1 Hz on average, with peak rates of 8 Hz) (GoodSmith et al., 2017; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017).
evidence: This is a physiological measurement from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: A more physiologically realistic stimulus pattern, in terms of both firing rate and timing, would reactivate memories more effectively.
source: We hypothesized that a more physiologically realistic stimulus pattern, in terms of both firing rate and timing, would reactivate memories more effectivity.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study.

claim: The algorithm reads the LFP from the CA1 region of the hippocampus and filters it using a finite impulse response filter between 4 and 10 Hz.
source: Our algorithm (Figure 1) reads the LFP from the CA1 region of the hippocampus and filters it using a finite impulse response filter between 4 and 10 Hz implemented in the Real-Time eXperimental Interface (RTXI) software (Lin et al., 2010; https://github.com/ndlBU/phase_specific_stim; Noueihed, 2022).
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study.

claim: The algorithm predicts the timing of the next desired extremum by averaging the duration of previous cycles.
source: The algorithm predicts the timing of the next desired extremum by averaging the duration of previous cycles and sends a TTL pulse to drive the laser at the predicted time of either the peak or the trough of the next theta cycle.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study.

claim: The phase of theta oscillations is in reference to measures in striatum pyramidale in the hippocampus.
source: The phase of theta oscillations is in reference to measures in striatum pyramidale in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the study.

claim: If the electrode location was observed to be in another layer of the hippocampus, the phase (trough vs. peak) was corrected to ensure similar theta phase across animals.
source: If the location of the electrode, as determined by post hoc histological analysis (see Methods), was observed to be in another layer of the hippocampus, we corrected for this change (trough vs. peak) to ensure similar theta phase across animals.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the study.

claim: The average frequency during both peak- and trough-specific stimulation was 6 Hz.
source: The average frequency during both peak- and trough-specific stimulation was 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: The use of closed-loop stimulation resulted in 83% and 84% true negative rate (specificity) for peak and trough stimulation, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 1Cii, the use of closed-loop stimulation resulted in significantly more phase-specific stimulation: 83%, 84% true negative rate (TNR, specificity) for peak and trough stimulation, respectively, as compared to 46% and 3% TNR with 6 Hz and 20 Hz stimulations, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study shown in Figure 1Cii.

claim: 6 Hz and 20 Hz stimulations resulted in 46% and 3% true negative rate, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 1Cii, the use of closed-loop stimulation resulted in significantly more phase-specific stimulation: 83%, 84% true negative rate (TNR, specificity) for peak and trough stimulation, respectively, as compared to 46% and 3% TNR with 6 Hz and 20 Hz stimulations, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study shown in Figure 1Cii.

claim: The algorithm has a low rate of stimulation outside of the desired phase.
source: These results indicate that our algorithm has a low rate of stimulation outside of the desired phase, which is critical to testing our hypothesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the specificity results.

claim: The sensitivity of the algorithm is moderately superior to the 6 Hz stimulation with a true positive rate of 58% and 59% for peak and trough, respectively, as compared to 54% for 6 Hz.
source: Moreover, sensitivity of the algorithm is moderately superior to the 6 Hz stimulation with a true positive rate (TPR) of 58% and 59% for peak and trough, respectively, as compared to 54% for 6 Hz.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study.

claim: 20 Hz stimulation results in a constant, non-specific stimulation with TNR and TPR of 3% and 97%, respectively.
source: Since a 20 Hz stimulation rate is about two times higher frequency than theta oscillations, it results in a constant, non-specific stimulation (TNR and TPR of 3% and 97%, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study with an explanation.

claim: The experimental setup was designed to test different modes of stimulation within the same animal.
source: We developed an experimental setup to compare phase-specific and fixed-frequency reactivation of hippocampal engram neurons. Importantly, our setup was designed to test different modes of stimulation within the same animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The experimental design randomized the order of the stimulation in different animals as repeated engram reactivation can affect the original memory.
source: Further, our experimental design randomized the order of the stimulation in different animals as repeated engram reactivation can affect the original memory.
evidence: This describes the experimental design with a rationale.

claim: The experiment took place in two different contexts: a neutral context A and a fearful context B.
source: The experiment took place in two different contexts: a neutral context A and a fearful context B.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Animals were first habituated to handling and exploration in the neutral context A over 4 days.
source: Animals were first habituated to handling and exploration in the neutral context A. Habituation took place over 4 days, during which both fiber optics and the LFP electrodes were attached to acclimatize the mice to the setup.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Light stimulation during habituation resulted in no behavioral change as no opsin was expressed yet.
source: Light stimulation took place, but as no opsin was expressed yet the light resulted in no behavioral change (Figure 2Cii).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2Cii.

claim: Animals were anxious on day 1 of habituation as shown by 15% freezing.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2Ci, the animals were anxious on day 1 as shown by the higher amount of freezing (15%).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: Animals quickly became habituated to the setup as shown by a much-reduced level of freezing (5%) on the last 2 days of habituation.
source: However, they quickly became habituated to the setup as shown by a much-reduced level of freezing on the last 2 days of the habituation (5%).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Each trial consisted of four 3 min epochs in which the stimulus lights were turned off and on in the order of No Stim, Stim, No Stim, Stim.
source: Each day, both during habituation and during the experiment, each animal had one trial consisting of four 3 min epochs in which the stimulus lights were turned off and on in the order of No Stim, Stim, No Stim, Stim.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Animal freezing on the last day of habituation was used as a measure of baseline freezing change for the rest of the experiment.
source: Animal freezing on the last day of habituation was used as a measure of baseline freezing change for the rest of the experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Freezing increased by about 5% during the trial on the last day of habituation.
source: As shown in Figure 2Cii, freezing increased by about 5% during the trial.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the study shown in Figure 2Cii.

claim: Animals were taken off doxycycline 48 hr prior to fear conditioning to allow for the tagging of engram neurons.
source: Following habituation, animals were taken off doxycycline 48 hr prior to fear conditioning to allow for the tagging of engram neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Experimental animals (FS+) received four 1.2 mA foot shocks during tagging, while control animals (FS-) were left to explore freely.
source: Over a second, 5 min interval, experimental animals (FS+) received four 1.2 mA foot shocks, while the control animals (FS-) were left to explore freely.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Both experimental and control animals showed minimal freezing prior to the shocks.
source: Both experimental and control animals showed minimal freezing prior to the shocks, with only experimental animals exhibiting elevated freezing after the foot shocks (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only experimental animals exhibited elevated freezing after the foot shocks.
source: Both experimental and control animals showed minimal freezing prior to the shocks, with only experimental animals exhibiting elevated freezing after the foot shocks (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only FS+ animals show an elevated level of freezing during recall, indicating successful recall of the fearful memory.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, only FS+ animals show an elevated level of freezing, indicating successful recall of the fearful memory.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2D with an interpretation.

claim: Post fear conditioning, only experimental animals showed elevated baseline freezing (1.5% pre vs 10% post), indicating a potential generalization of the fearful context B memory to the neutral context A.
source: Following tagging and recall of the fearful memory in context B, animals were re-exposed to the neutral context A in which they were originally habituated. Post fear conditioning, only experimental animals showed elevated baseline freezing (1.5% pre vs 10% post), indicating a potential generalization of the fearful context B memory to the neutral context A (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 2E with an interpretation.

claim: Neutral context A freezing (10%) was lower than the freezing following fear conditioning (45%) or during recall (46%) of the fearful memory in context B.
source: Despite the elevated freezing (10%), neutral context A freezing was lower than the freezing following fear conditioning (45%) or during recall (46%) of the fearful memory in context B (Figure 2D vs. 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the study shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: The increased baseline freezing obscured the light-induced freezing and required the artificial memory reactivation to generate higher freezing levels to be deemed effective.
source: However, the increased baseline freezing in neutral context A obscured the light-induced freezing and, therefore, required the artificial memory reactivation to generate higher freezing levels to be deemed effective.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental conditions.

claim: The elevated baseline freezing is similar across days, making it possible to pool data from different days.
source: It is important to note that the elevated baseline freezing is similar across days, making it possible to pool data from different days.
evidence: This is a justification for the data analysis approach.

claim: Only stimulation at the trough of theta could drive the expected increase in freezing during both stimulation epochs.
source: As shown in Figure 3Ai, only stimulation at the trough of theta could drive the expected increase in freezing during both stimulation epochs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study shown in Figure 3Ai.

claim: 6 Hz stimulation was effective during the first stimulation epoch but failed to elicit significant freezing during the second epoch.
source: Although 6 Hz stimulation was effective during the first stimulation epoch, this frequency failed to elicit significant freezing during the second epoch.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Peak and 20 Hz stimulations showed a gradual increase in freezing that was similar to the habituation trial.
source: Peak and 20 Hz stimulations showed a gradual increase in freezing that was similar to the habituation trial.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Only trough stimulation resulted in significantly higher freezing rates when averaging light-induced freezing across epochs.
source: Averaging the light-induced freezing across epochs indicated that only trough stimulation resulted in significantly higher freezing rates (Figure 3Aii; paired t-test, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study shown in Figure 3Aii with statistical analysis.

claim: Only trough stimulation elicits light-induced freezing values significantly different than the habituation trials.
source: Further, paired comparisons of the amount of light-induced freezing during each stimulation indicated that only trough stimulation elicits light-induced freezing values significantly different than the habituation trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in freezing in the cases of peak stimulation, as well as 20 Hz and 6 Hz fixed-frequency stimulations, were like those expected from a general increase in the animal's immobility in later trials.
source: As a result, the increase in freezing in the cases of peak stimulation, as well as 20 Hz and 6 Hz fixed-frequency stimulations, were like those expected from a general increase in the animal's immobility in later trials (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Direct comparisons of trough and peak stimulations within each animal showed significantly higher freezing values when using trough stimulation.
source: Direct comparisons of trough and peak stimulations within each animal showed significantly higher freezing values when using trough stimulation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Activating engram neurons at the trough of theta was more effective at inducing artificial recall of a tagged memory.
source: The analysis indicated that activating engram neurons at the trough of theta was more effective at inducing artificial recall of a tagged memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The experimental group showed significantly higher freezing post reactivation of engrams in the neutral context A, indicating a potential strengthening of the original tagged memory.
source: We also found that the experimental group showed significantly higher freezing post reactivation of engrams in the neutral context A, which we believe indicates a potential strengthening of the original tagged memory.
evidence: This is an observation with an interpretation.

claim: Theta oscillations were higher in frequency during locomotion when compared with measurements made during freezing.
source: Consistent with previous studies, theta oscillations were higher in frequency during locomotion (Figure 4B, see the 'bumps' in the blue lines in the right panels) when compared with measurements made during freezing (red lines).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 4B, consistent with prior literature.

claim: This trend held during all epochs of the experiment regardless of the presence or absence of the stimulation.
source: This trend held during all epochs of the experiment regardless of the presence or absence of the stimulation.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Theta power is not significantly different in freezing vs. non-freezing conditions.
source: A more detailed analysis of theta power (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) demonstrates that theta power is not significantly different in freezing vs. non-freezing conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 30–100 Hz gamma rhythm has been theorized to play a critical role in hippocampal memory processing.
source: The 30–100 Hz gamma rhythm has been theorized to play a critical role in hippocampal memory processing (Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about a theoretical model supported by citation.

claim: Theta-gamma coherence is correlated with coordinated information transfer between different sub-regions of the hippocampus.
source: Electrophysiological studies have established that theta-gamma coherence is correlated with coordinated information transfer between different sub-regions of the hippocampus (Pernía-Andrade and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from prior studies supported by citation.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling has been demonstrated in a memory test experiment that established a correlation between the strength of this coupling and memory performance.
source: Moreover, cross-frequency coupling (CFC) has been demonstrated in a memory test experiment that established a correlation between the strength of this coupling and memory performance (Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: The MI was highest between the phase of theta filtered at 4–8 Hz frequency and the amplitude of 55–85 Hz gamma, known as mid-gamma.
source: Our analysis indicated that the MI was highest between the phase of theta filtered at 4–8 Hz frequency and the amplitude of 55–85 Hz gamma, known as mid-gamma.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Comparing the MI at baseline (pre-stimulation epoch) indicated no difference between the four stimulation patterns.
source: Comparing the MI at baseline (pre-stimulation epoch) indicated no difference between the four stimulation patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: During the stimulation period, only trough activation showed elevated values in MI, which then went back to control levels during the post-stimulation period.
source: However, during the stimulation period, only trough activation showed elevated values in MI, which then went back to control levels during the post-stimulation period (epoch 3, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The MI was only significantly modulated in cases using trough stimulation, which was significantly higher than both pre- and post-stimulation.
source: Comparing pre-stimulation to stimulation epochs for each mouse confirmed that the MI was only significantly modulated in cases using trough stimulation, which was significantly higher than both pre- and post-stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: In other stimulation setups, no differences in the MI were observed between the three epochs.
source: In other stimulation setups, we observed no differences in the MI between the three epochs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5C.

claim: With trough stimulation, the behavioral response was stronger (higher light-induced freezing) and the MI was higher.
source: Consistent with the SPEAR model, our data support the hypothesis that the peak and trough of theta correspond to different modes of hippocampal function with regard to memory processing. In particular, we observed that with trough stimulation the behavioral response was stronger (higher light-induced freezing) and that the MI was higher (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5D with an interpretation.

claim: With peak stimulation, the relationship between behavioral response and MI was in the opposite direction, albeit not at a significant level.
source: This relationship was in the opposite direction, albeit not at a significant level, when using stimulation at the peak of theta (Figure 5D, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The result did not hold for slow gamma.
source: Surprisingly, this result did not hold for slow gamma (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), as we would have expected from the literature related to natural recall (Colgin, 2015; Colgin, 2016; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Schomburg et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, with reference to expectations from prior literature.

claim: Activating DG memory neurons during the trough of the theta field potential is most effective at inducing recall of stored memories and yields the most robust behavioral outcome.
source: Using c-fos-dependent neuronal tagging of cells associated with fear conditioning, as well as theta-phase-specific photo-stimulation, we assessed the functional role of theta phase in memory processing. We show that activating DG memory neurons during the trough of the theta field potential is most effective at inducing recall of stored memories and yields the most robust behavioral outcome corresponding to successful artificial reactivation of the tagged memory.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: When artificial recall is elicited through phase-specific stimulation, the behavioral outcome is well correlated with an increase in phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma oscillations.
source: When artificial recall is elicited through phase-specific stimulation, the behavioral outcome is well correlated with an increase in phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma oscillations, which has been established as an electrophysiological correlate of memory performance (Kragel et al., 2020; Tort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study with reference to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies have observed frequency dependence in eliciting behavioral responses across different regions of the hippocampus.
source: Previous studies have observed frequency dependence in eliciting behavioral responses across different regions of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research.

claim: Ryan et al., 2015, activated CA1 memory neurons using 4 Hz optogenetic stimulation and observed consistent behavioral responses.
source: For example, Ryan et al., 2015, activated CA1 memory neurons using 4 Hz optogenetic stimulation and observed consistent behavioral responses, while Ohkawa et al., 2015, were able to drive behavior with 20 Hz stimulation in the same region.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: Ohkawa et al., 2015, were able to drive behavior with 20 Hz stimulation in CA1.
source: For example, Ryan et al., 2015, activated CA1 memory neurons using 4 Hz optogenetic stimulation and observed consistent behavioral responses, while Ohkawa et al., 2015, were able to drive behavior with 20 Hz stimulation in the same region.
evidence: This is a finding from a prior study supported by citation.

claim: The majority of past studies have used 20 Hz stimulation to drive engram activation in DG despite the rate being much higher than natural DG granule cell firing rates in vivo.
source: In the case of DG, the majority of past studies have used 20 Hz stimulation to drive engram activation despite the rate being much higher than natural DG granule cell firing rates in vivo (GoodSmith et al., 2017; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about prior research methods supported by citations.

claim: The results support the SPEAR model and a general role for theta oscillations in organizing memory recall in the hippocampus.
source: Overall, our results support the SPEAR model (Hasselmo et al., 2002), as well as a general role for theta oscillations in organizing memory recall in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The effectiveness of trough stimulation in eliciting recall is consistent with previous experiments in rodents and human subjects performing memory tasks.
